item.title: Fijian rapist to be deported from Australia after 16-year sentence
item.description: A Fijian national attempted to flee the country after a horror sex attack on a disabled woman described by a judge as “every woman’s worst nightmare”. Samuela Turaganivalu, 34, was jailed for more than 16 years in the County Court on Tuesday for breaking into a stranger’s home and raping her.
item.content:encoded:
A Fijian national attempted to flee the country after a horror sex attack on a disabled woman described by a judge as “every woman’s worst nightmare”.

Samuela Turaganivalu, 34, was jailed for more than 16 years in the County Court on Tuesday for breaking into a stranger’s home and raping her.

Handing down the sentence, Judge Gerard Mullaly described Turaganivalu’s actions in the early hours of the morning on November 17, 2024, as “heinous, frightening behaviour”.

“This is every woman’s nightmare,” the judge said.

“That someone with criminal, violent intent breaks into their house, overpowering them and raping them.”

Turaganivalu, the court was told, had arrived in Australia on an employment program two years earlier to work on farms and in factories.

Judge Mullaly said shortly after midnight on November 17, Turaganivalu met up with a woman he was dating for drinks at a hotel before the woman left without him.

In the hours that followed, Turaganivalu was “constantly” trying to get in contact with the woman via phone and showed up at a home he wrongly believed she was inside of.

After failing to gain entry, he tore the side mirrors off a car before climbing over the back fence of a neighbouring home and entering through an unlocked door.

Inside, Judge Mullaly said, Turaganivalu woke and “brutally attacked” his victim, punching her in the face multiple times.

The “powerful, large man” then anally raped her before threatening he would come back and kill her if she called the police.

The judge said it was indicative of the “utter terror” the victim was in that she complied and did not call police but alerted a friend who then called triple-0.

Turaganivalu was initially only identified as the perpetrator of the damage to the car and was arrested the following day, interviewed and released from custody.

On November 19, he was arrested at Melbourne airport with a one-way ticket to Fiji.

The convicted rapist was found guilty in June following a jury trial in which he denied the rape occurred but admitted he assaulted the woman.

“Plainly, the jury rejected your account,” Judge Mullaly said.

The court was told Turaganivalu had no prior convictions in Australia or Fiji, was raised in a loving family and was a talented rugby player.

Judge Mullaly said the woman had physical and intellectual disabilities, and Turaganivalu’s crimes had stolen her independence and confidence.

“I wish I could have my old life back, but I cannot,” the woman said.

She told the court she had to give up a job she loved because she was now “too frightened to come home in the dark”.

Her parents said they were proud of her “hard won and deeply cherished” independence, but Turaganivalu’s actions had “changed her life forever”.

“They spent a lifetime building their daughter’s independence only for you Mr Turaganivalu to dismantle their efforts in one night,” Judge Mullaly said.

“Her parents have had to assist her more that previously because she now lacks confidence.

“You, of course, are the only one to blame for that.”

Turaganivalu was sentenced to 16 years and four months, with a non-parole period of 12 years and will “almost certainly” be deported following the end of his jail term, the court was told.

He did not visibly react as the sentence was handed down.

item.title: MP Sanjay Kirpal, co-accused granted bail
item.description: Member of Parliament Sanjay Kirpal and another man accused of assaulting a man on August 9 have been granted bail. Mr Kirpal and Anal Avinash Ram appeared before Magistrate Shageeth Somaratne for the first time this afternoon, charged with one count of assault.
item.content:encoded:
Member of Parliament Sanjay Kirpal and another man accused of assaulting a man on August 9 have been granted bail.

Mr Kirpal and Anal Avinash Ram appeared before Magistrate Shageeth Somaratne for the first time this afternoon, charged with one count of assault.

The pair are alleged to have assaulted the complainant following an argument at Kirpal’s home.

Their lawyer, Mukesh Nand, told the court that both accused were willing to reconcile with the complainant.

The court heard that the accused and the complainant do not have a domestic relationship.

Police prosecutor Sergeant Shailend Prasad, when asked by the magistrate whether the complainant was also willing to reconcile, said he could not confirm this at the moment.

Magistrate Somaratne directed Sergeant Prasad to confirm with the complainant whether he was willing to reconcile.

The magistrate said if there was no reconciliation, the accused would have their pleas recorded on the next court date.

item.title: Liberation of Fiji Party registered, bringing total political parties to 11
item.description: Liberation of Fiji Party Registered, Bringing Total Political Parties to 11 The Liberation of Fiji Party (LFP) has been officially registered as a political party, bringing the total number of registered political parties in Fiji to 11.
item.content:encoded:
Liberation of Fiji Party Registered, Bringing Total Political Parties to 11

The Liberation of Fiji Party (LFP) has been officially registered as a political party, bringing the total number of registered political parties in Fiji to 11.

Registrar of Political Parties Ana Mataiciwa approved the LFP’s registration under the Political Parties (Registration, Conduct, Funding and Disclosures) Act 2013.

The Registrar confirmed the party had met all legal requirements for registration under the Act.

The LFP resubmitted its application on July 20, 2026, after its initial application was not approved on July 3.

As a newly registered political party, the LFP is required to comply with all statutory obligations under the Act, including submitting the relevant declarations and disclosures within the prescribed timelines.

The registration comes as political parties continue to position themselves ahead of Fiji’s next general election.

With the LFP now registered, the number of political parties officially registered in Fiji stands at 11.

item.title: High Court to hear challenge over seizure of devices
item.description: A High Court application challenging a search warrant used to retain seven electronic devices belonging to Citizen Journalist Charlie Charter will be heard on Monday. The matter was called before Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu today.
item.content:encoded:
A High Court application challenging a search warrant used to retain seven electronic devices belonging to Citizen Journalist Charlie Charter will be heard on Monday.

The matter was called before Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu today.

Defence lawyer Juleen Fatiaki of Fatiaki Law said the seven devices had been seized by police on August 7, after Mr Charter’s solicitor, Seforan Fatiaki, attended the Criminal Investigations Department to uplift the devices following an order by the Magistrates’ Court for their release.

However, Mr Fatiaki was served with a search warrant and the devices were retained by police.

The defence argues the devices contain confidential and privileged material and has invoked Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

Ms Fatiaki also told the court the information used to obtain the warrant did not indicate its relevance to Charter’s case, apart from listing the devices owned by him.

The court also heard that the search warrant was signed by Magistrate Sufia Hamza. When the judge asked Ms Fatiaki whether the magistrate was aware of his permanent stay ruling, Ms Fatiaki said she had no information on that.

The Commissioner of Police had yet to be served with the application.

Justice Bulamainaivalu directed that the motion and affidavit be served on the Commissioner of Police before Monday’s hearing.

item.title: Leona on a mission to empower youths
item.description: At 21, Leona Douglas is stepping onto the Hibiscus stage with a purpose that goes beyond the crown — to speak up for those who cannot speak or be seen, and to use the platform to create opportunities for Fiji’s youth. Born in New Zealand and raised in Fiji, Ms Leona moved with her family to Taveuni as a young child before settling in Suva, where she completed her schooling.
item.content:encoded:
At 21, Leona Douglas is stepping onto the Hibiscus stage with a purpose that goes beyond the crown — to speak up for those who cannot speak or be seen, and to use the platform to create opportunities for Fiji’s youth.

Born in New Zealand and raised in Fiji, Ms Leona moved with her family to Taveuni as a young child before settling in Suva, where she completed her schooling.

Her journey growing up in Fiji has shaped her belief that young people are central to the country’s future.

“The youth are our future here in Fiji, and they possess immense talent capable of taking us one step further,” she said.

Through the Miss Hibiscus platform, Leona hopes to empower young people, bridge gaps and shine a light on their potential.

Joining the pageant was initially daunting, with Leona admitting she was nervous about having “all eyes on you most of the time”.

After reflecting on her reasons for entering, she decided to put her fears aside and focus on those who could benefit from the platform.

“I chose to think about the people who need this platform, those who will benefit from it.”

item.title: Calls for holistic approach
item.description: THE Fiji Navy is calling for greater focus on preventing maritime emergencies, saying search-and-rescue efforts should not rely only on responding after people get into trouble at sea. In an interview yesterday, Fiji Navy Commander Timoci Natuva said the navy was often at the back end of the response and that more needed to be done before incidents occurred.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Navy is calling for greater focus on preventing maritime emergencies, saying search-and-rescue efforts should not rely only on responding after people get into trouble at sea.

In an interview yesterday, Fiji Navy Commander Timoci Natuva said the navy was often at the back end of the response and that more needed to be done before incidents occurred.

“For search-and-rescue, we have to take, just like drugs, a holistic approach to addressing it,” he said.

He said greater awareness in the islands was needed, including ensuring people consider weather conditions and take appropriate action before going out to sea.

Commander Natuva said the next priority was the response itself, including how quickly and accurately information is passed to the relevant agencies.

“The co-ordination and having the assets ready to deploy, having the right funds to support those operations.”

He said funding had been difficult during the last two search-and-rescue operations in the Lau waters because they came towards the end of the financial year.

“Australia had supported the navy with fuel during the operations.”

Commander Natuva said the navy was also reviewing how safety information is communicated to vessels, including whether existing radio broadcasts are reaching seafarers.

“We are readjusting and reviewing those systems.”

He said the navy was considering whether high frequency radio should continue to be used for safety calls or whether text messages could be used given that most boats now use modern communication systems.

Commander Natuva said prevention and a faster, better-co-ordinated response were both necessary to strengthen Fiji’s search-and-rescue efforts.

item.title: US hands Fiji three new boats to fight threats
item.description: Fiji is strengthening its frontline response to drug trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats in its waters with the handover of three new seven-metre rigid-hull inflatable boats and a boat ramp from the US. The equipment were formally handed over at the Stanley Brown Naval Base, with US Chargé d’Affaires Christina Cavallo saying the boats would help Fiji confront growing transnational threa
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is strengthening its frontline response to drug trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats in its waters with the handover of three new seven-metre rigid-hull inflatable boats and a boat ramp from the US.

The equipment were formally handed over at the Stanley Brown Naval Base, with US Chargé d’Affaires Christina Cavallo saying the boats would help Fiji confront growing transnational threats across the Pacific.

“Whether seizing tonnes of methamphetamine from shipping containers or finding bundles of cocaine washed up on our beaches, we all grapple with illegal drug trafficking,” Ms Cavallo said.

The boats, she said, would also support fisheries enforcement, search-and-rescue and efforts to protect Fiji’s sovereignty and maritime resources.

Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said the boats were important because Fiji is an ocean state, with its trade, people, fisheries and remote communities dependent on the sea which makes maritime capability critical.

“These rigs may be small vessels, but they will give the navy greater flexibility and mobility in the work it does,” he said.

Mr Tikoduadua said the boats would allow sailors to operate closer to shore, move personnel quickly and undertake tasks for which larger vessels were not always suited.

“Fiji must be able to understand what is happening in our waters, to act when required, and to contribute meaningfully to the security of our region.”

Fiji Navy Commander Timoci Natuva said the project had been in development with the US since 2018-2019 and is intended to increase the navy’s presence across Fiji’s waters.

Commander Natuva said the growing threat from drugs and recent cases had increased the need for a stronger presence in Fiji’s waters.

“So, this will be very important in terms of getting our footprint out through Fiji in the islands,” he said.

Commander Natuva said the US support included the boats, infrastructure, training and parts, and described it as a “complete package”.

He said the boats would support presence, interdiction, boarding operations, search-and- rescue in close proximity to land.
